turn_text: I wanted to ask you a question about the COVID pandemic. I know that I have a few friends that are pregnant and were telling me that they hadn't actually been to the doctor the way they normally would have. I had a friend who wasn't actually able to make it in until her 20 week ultrasound. And of course she had virtual check-ins with her doctors, but are you concerned that maternity care is suffering at all during the pandemic?

Yes, I have spoken to providers that told me, for example, They wanted to shift so many of their expectant moms to these virtual visits, but everybody couldn't afford a blood pressure cuff. And if you haven't been diagnosed with preeclampsia, then you know, oftentimes insurers will not pay for that blood pressure cuff because there's no clinical need, right? But what we want to do is prevent someone from getting pregnancy-related high blood pressure. And because we know that that is such a key risk factor to, you know, maternal morbidity and mortality, right? And so there are challenges in this COVID-19 space with transitioning to telehealth, with making sure that women are getting that kind of support that they need. And quite frankly, recognizing that that tele-visit, that telehealth exchange is not necessarily the evidence-based intervention that we can count on to save mom's lives during this critical period. And so again, I pride myself on being a data-driven evidence-based policymaker. I like to consult with the biomedical research and evidence, talk with my nursing colleagues and our physician colleagues to make sure that the community groups, obviously, that the legislation that we're putting forward has its roots in the evidence that would work to save mom's lives. And I think in this COVID era, we need to make sure that everything that we're doing is not just for convenience, but that there is a clinical effectiveness that goes along with it. And I think that there's some work still to be done in that telehealth space.
